exam_title: Debugging Error Test — Easy (IBPS SO IT Mains)
subject: Debugging
question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int x = 0; if (x = 0) printf("yes"); else printf("no");
option_c: A compile-time error, because an assignment cannot appear in a condition
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The condition uses assignment, not comparison, so x is set to 0 and the condition value is 0. A zero condition is false, so the else branch prints no. Remember: one equal sign in a condition assigns, and a zero result does not enter the if body.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Count the equal signs inside the condition. One equal sign is not a comparison.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The condition is legal C. It does not print both words, and it does not take the true branch.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: one equal sign in a condition assigns, and a zero result does not enter the if body.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int i; for (i = 0; i < 5; i++); printf("%d", i);
option_d: A compile-time error, because a for loop cannot end with a semicolon
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The semicolon is an empty loop body, so the loop only increments i until the test fails. The test fails when i is 5, and that is the value printed after the loop. Remember: a semicolon after the for header means the following statement is not the loop body.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Look at the semicolon immediately after the for header.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The loop is legal. Its body is empty, so it does not print 01234, and i does not stop at 4.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a semicolon after the for header means the following statement is not the loop body.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? switch (1) { case 1: printf("A"); case 2: printf("B"); break; default: printf("C"); }
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: A switch falls through to the next case when break is missing, so case 1 prints A and case 2 then prints B. The break after B stops the switch before default. Remember: without break, matching a case is not the end of the switch.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. There is no break at the end of the matching case.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Execution does not stop after A, and it does not reach default, because a break appears before default. It also does not start at case 2.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: without break, matching a case is not the end of the switch.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? printf("%d", 3 + 4 * 2);
option_b: A compile-time error, because the expression mixes + and *
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so the expression is 3 plus 8, which is 11. Left-to-right addition would be the wrong rule here. Remember: * happens before + unless parentheses say otherwise.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Multiplication and addition are not done strictly left to right.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. 14 would be (3 + 4) * 2. 24 is not a reading of this expression. The expression is legal.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: * happens before + unless parentheses say otherwise.

question: Debugging error test. What is wrong with this fragment? int a[5]; a[5] = 10;
option_a: The array cannot be declared with a size of 5
option_b: The assignment is a compile-time type error
option_c: Index 5 is outside the legal indexes, which run from 0 through 4
option_d: Nothing is wrong, because the last legal index of an array of 5 is 5
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: An array of 5 elements has indexes 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, so a[5] is past the end. C often will not reject that write at compile time, but the write is out of bounds. Remember: the last legal index is size minus 1.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Count the legal indexes of a five-element array. They do not start at 1.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The declaration is legal, and the assignment has a legal type. The problem is which index is named.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: the last legal index is size minus 1.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int n = 5; printf("%d", n / 2 * 2);
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: Integer division truncates, so 5 divided by 2 is 2, and that intermediate result times 2 is 4. The expression is not a rounding back to 5. Remember: left to right, int divided by int drops the fraction before the multiply.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. The operators have the same precedence and associate left to right. Do the division first.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The result is an int, so 2.5 is not printed. 5 would require the division to keep a fraction. 2 is only the intermediate quotient.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: left to right, int divided by int drops the fraction before the multiply.

question: Debugging error test. What is wrong with this loop? int i = 0; while (i < 3) { printf("%d", i); }
option_a: The loop variable is never incremented, so the loop does not terminate
option_b: A while loop cannot contain printf
option_c: i is compared with the wrong type
option_d: The loop body is skipped because i starts at 0
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The body prints i but never changes i, so i remains 0 and the condition remains true. The loop therefore does not terminate. Remember: a while condition that never becomes false is an infinite loop.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Ask what changes inside the body. The condition uses i.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. printf is legal in a loop. The comparison is an int compared with an int. The body is entered because 0 is less than 3.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a while condition that never becomes false is an infinite loop.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int x = 7; printf("%d", x % 2);
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The percent operator yields the remainder, and 7 divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 1. An even value would leave 0. Remember: n percent 2 is 0 for even n and 1 for positive odd n.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. The percent operator is the remainder, not a percentage.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. 7 is odd, so the remainder on division by 2 is not 0. It is not 3, and it is not the divisor.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: n percent 2 is 0 for even n and 1 for positive odd n.
